doc.title: Oliver Nelson Jr. interviewed by Monk Rowe, via Zoom, September 10, 2020

title: Pandemic effects on rehearsals and clubs
summary: Zoom-era distancing for ensembles, a Brent Wallarab concert of his father's music, and clubs banning horns and vocalists.

story.theme_name: Where jazz stands today: young players, rock, and the audience
story.community_name: How the music business changed: hype, youth and lost apprenticeship

blocks.x: I see. What’s in the near — I have to stop this question. I was going to say what’s in the near future, but none of us know.
We don’t know. I’m supposed to —
We’re all in sort of this Zoom world and some of us are making it through better than others I guess.

Well it’s interesting, a guy named Brent Wallarab, he’s one that teaches at IU, he teaches arranging and composition and stuff. He’s doing this concert of my dad’s music and asked me to play on it. And I wanted some of my jazz for listening students to come. Well I talked to the head of the department and he said well I have to check and see. Because they might not let you. And these guys were having rehearsals, and everybody is so separated. So he’s trying to put them in clusters kind of close together so you can get a blend. Because you can’t get a blend anymore. The orchestra down there, all those guys are doing Zoom. The jazz guys with the big bands are able to have rehearsals but the whole room is all spread out.
You know I have a nine member saxophone ensemble and they constantly are slowing down. And I’m going what’s the problem. Well there’s 60 feet from one end to the other.
So how do you hear? You can’t hear. I was looking at the Green Mill in Chicago, great jazz club, they opened back up and they said you know what? No horn players and no vocalists.

Well I thought it was the Green Mill because the Green Mill did the same thing too. But no vocalists and no horn players. So how are you going to run a club like that? But you know what you’re blessed, Monk. I fell I’m blessed too, to be able to have a teaching gig.

I mean that brings still money into your coffers and that’s a good thing to have and today, like you said, you’ve got tons of guys — I remember ten years ago they would not allow a doctor of jazz studies. Now there’s a ton of them. And everybody’s looking for work.
